hops.afterHeading: Count before you divide: homologs, sisters and ploidy
hops.title: Two look-alike deer with 46 and 6 chromosomes
hops.text: Muntjacs are small Asian deer, also called barking deer. The Chinese muntjac and the Indian muntjac look alike, and they can mate and have live hybrid fawns. Now count their centromeres. The Chinese muntjac has 46 chromosomes in both sexes, the same number as you. The Indian muntjac has 6 in females and 7 in males: in its line, ancestral chromosomes fused into a few giant ones. Yet the two species carry similar amounts of DNA per haploid set, 2.7 picograms in the Chinese muntjac and 2.1 in the Indian. A chromosome count tells you how the DNA is packaged, not how much there is.

sources.citation: Tsipouri et al., Genome Biology 9(10):R155 (2008), PMC2760882.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two small reddish-brown deer standing side by side on a mossy forest path among ferns, looking at each other.
image.caption: Chinese and Indian muntjacs look alike and hold similar DNA, yet carry 46 versus 6 or 7 chromosomes.

hops.afterHeading: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sisters
hops.title: Why a supermarket banana has no seeds
hops.text: Next time you peel a banana, snap it in half and look down the middle. Those tiny brown flecks are the remains of ovules, the structures that would have become seeds. Wild bananas are diploid, and their fruit is packed with hard, gravelly seeds. Cavendish and most other dessert bananas are triploid: three sets of 11, or 33 chromosomes. At anaphase I, three homologs cannot split evenly between two poles, so meiosis often makes gametes with unbalanced sets. That, with sterility genes and rearranged chromosomes, means seeds rarely form. The fruit grows anyway, without fertilization, and growers propagate the plants as clones.

sources.citation: Heslop-Harrison & Schwarzacher, Annals of Botany 100(5):1073-1084 (2007), PMC2759213.
Miao et al., Horticulture Research 12(5):uhaf044 (2025), PMC11997438.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Hands breaking a peeled yellow banana in half over a wooden counter, showing tiny brown specks in the center.
image.caption: The brown flecks are ovules that never became seeds; three chromosome sets help keep Cavendish bananas seedless.

hops.afterHeading: Crossing over: what holds the pair, and what it does to alleles
hops.title: A Romanian jawbone with a recent Neanderthal ancestor
hops.text: In 2002, a human jawbone turned up in a Romanian cave called Peștera cu Oase. It is 37,000 to 42,000 years old. When geneticists read its DNA in 2015, they estimated that 6 to 9 percent was Neanderthal, far more than the 1 to 3 percent in present-day Eurasians, and some Neanderthal stretches were unusually long. Crossing over swaps pieces between non-sister chromatids, so over the generations, long stretches from any one ancestor tend to get broken up. From those long stretches, the team estimated a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back, less than 200 years before this man lived: possibly as close as a great-great-grandparent.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A weathered fossil lower jawbone on dark linen beside a small wooden brush and a brass magnifying glass.
image.caption: In 2015, long Neanderthal stretches in an ancient Romanian jawbone suggested a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back.
